title: Antiochus IV takes Jerusalem and stops the daily sacrifice
native: in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes; sacrifice stopped “for three years and six months”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 167 BC (Kislev 167 BC per 1 Macc 1:54); the city was first sacked c. 168 BC.
note: Antiochus IV plundered the Temple and halted the daily sacrifice; War gives 3½ years, where 1 Maccabees counts 3 years (167–164 BC).

title: Onias flees to Egypt and builds a temple at Heliopolis (Leontopolis)
native: after Antiochus's war; in “the Nomus of Heliopolis”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Scholars date the foundation c. 170–150 BC; Josephus's '343 years' to its closure (7.10.4) would imply an impossible earlier date.
note: The high priest Onias built a rival Jewish temple in Egypt with Ptolemy's leave; it stood until Vespasian had it closed (War 7.10).

title: Judas Maccabeus cleanses the Temple and builds a new altar
native: after Judas drove out Epiphanes
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 25 Kislev 164 BC (from 1 Maccabees, not War).
note: Judas recaptured the Temple, purified it, and restarted the sacrifices; this rededication is the origin of Hanukkah.

title: Eleazar Maccabee killed beneath a war elephant at Beth-zechariah
native: when Antiochus [V] marched through Judea
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 162 BC.
note: Judas's brother Eleazar stabbed the royal elephant thinking the king rode it, and was crushed; the Jews lost the battle.

title: Death of Judas Maccabeus in battle
native: after the battle with Bacchides' forces
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 160 BC.
note: Judas fell fighting the Seleucid army; leadership passed to his brothers Jonathan and then Simon.

title: Simon the Hasmonean murdered at a feast by his son-in-law Ptolemy
native: “slain at a feast by his son-in-law Ptolemy”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 1 Macc 16:14 dates it Shebat, 177 SE = early 134 BC; War gives no date.
note: Simon was killed with his two sons; his son John Hyrcanus escaped to Jerusalem and took the high priesthood.

title: A sabbatical year ends Hyrcanus's siege of Dagon
native: “the year of rest came on, upon which the Jews rest every seventh year as they do on every seventh day”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Scholars place this sabbatical year at 135/134 BC (Zuckermann) or 134/133 BC (Wacholder).
note: The sabbatical year halted Hyrcanus's siege; Ptolemy killed Hyrcanus's mother and brothers and fled. A dated sabbatical year useful for sabbath/jubilee cycles.

title: John Hyrcanus besieges and takes Samaria
native: Samaria, “where is now the city Sebaste”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Usually dated c. 108/107 BC.
note: Hyrcanus's sons Aristobulus and Antigonus besieged Samaria, beat Antiochus Cyzicenus, and razed the city.

title: John Hyrcanus dies after 33 years of rule
native: “this for thirty-three entire years together”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 104 BC (reign 135/134–104 BC).
note: Josephus calls Hyrcanus the one man who held rule, high priesthood and the gift of prophecy together.

title: Aristobulus I is the first Hasmonean to wear a royal diadem
native: “four hundred seventy and one years and three months after our people came down into this country… from the Babylonian slavery”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 104 BC; his reign lasted one year.
note: Aristobulus turned the high-priestly rule into a kingdom, jailed his brothers and starved his mother. Josephus's 471 years from the return is a chronology anchor to compare with others.

title: Judas the Essene's prophecy fulfilled: Antigonus killed at Strato's Tower
native: at “that festival, wherein our ancient custom is to make tabernacles for God”
conversion: Festival of Tabernacles (15–21 Tishri); year c. 104/103 BC from the one-year reign of Aristobulus I.
note: Judas, an Essene who 'had never failed' in his predictions, foretold Antigonus's death at 'Strato's Tower'; Antigonus was killed in an underground passage of that name in Jerusalem.

title: Alexander Jannaeus attacked by the people at a festival; 6,000 slain
native: “at a festival; for at those feasts seditions are generally begun”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. 94–90 BC; War names no festival, Antiquities 13.13.5 says Tabernacles.
note: The nation rose against Jannaeus at a feast and his mercenaries killed more than 6,000; Antiquities says it was Tabernacles. A six-year civil war followed.

title: Alexander Jannaeus crucifies 800 opponents in Jerusalem
native: after the defeat of Demetrius [III]
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Usually dated c. 88 BC.
note: Jannaeus hung 800 Jews on crosses and killed their families before them while he feasted. The Qumran Nahum Pesher (4Q169) appears to recall this 'Lion of Wrath' who 'hangs men alive'.

title: Queen Alexandra reigns; the Pharisees gain power
native: after Alexander's death
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Reign 76–67 BC.
note: Alexandra let the Pharisees control affairs; they had Jannaeus's advisers killed.

title: Pompey takes the Temple after a three-month siege
native: “it was in the third month of the siege” that the Romans broke into the Temple; Pompey raised his banks on “the seventh days”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 63 BC is secure. War gives only 'the third month of the siege'; Antiquities 14.4.3 adds the 'fast day' and the 179th Olympiad (consuls Antonius and Cicero).
note: Pompey built his siege works on Sabbaths, when the Jews only defended themselves. Priests kept sacrificing as they were killed; 12,000 Jews died, and Pompey entered the Holy of Holies.

title: Gabinius divides Judea into five councils
native: under Gabinius
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. 57 BC.
note: Gabinius kept Hyrcanus as high priest only and set up five councils at Jerusalem, Gadara, Amathus, Jericho and Sepphoris.

title: Crassus strips the Temple of its gold
native: “Crassus came as successor to Gabinius in Syria”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 54 BC; Crassus died at Carrhae in 53 BC.
note: Crassus took the Temple gold, including the 2,000 talents Pompey had left, for his Parthian campaign, where he died.

title: Julius Caesar makes Antipater procurator of Judea
native: after the Alexandrian war
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 47 BC.
note: Caesar rewarded Antipater's help in Egypt with Roman citizenship and appointed him procurator, confirming Hyrcanus as high priest.

title: Antipater, Herod's father, poisoned by Malichus
native: under Cassius
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 43 BC.
note: Malichus bribed Hyrcanus's butler to poison Antipater; Herod later had Malichus killed with Cassius's consent.

title: Herod enters Jerusalem armed at the Pentecost festival
native: “at the [Pentecost] festival, he returned to Jerusalem”
conversion: Pentecost falls in Sivan; year 43 or 42 BC.
note: Herod brought foreign troops into the city at night despite Hyrcanus's ban during the festival purifications.

title: Parthians invade at Pentecost; Antigonus seizes the throne
native: “when that festival which we call Pentecost was at hand”
conversion: Pentecost falls in Sivan; 40 BC.
note: With the city full of armed pilgrims, the Parthians came in under cover of mediating. Phasael died in captivity, Hyrcanus's ears were cut off, and Herod escaped to Masada and then to Rome.

title: The Roman Senate names Herod king of the Jews
native: Antony “resolved to get him made king of the Jews”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Late 40 BC (Antiquities: 184th Olympiad, consuls Calvinus and Pollio).
note: On Antony's motion, backed by Octavian, the Senate declared Herod king and Antigonus an enemy of Rome. Josephus counts Herod's 37 years from here.

title: Herod and Sosius take Jerusalem after a five-month siege
native: “as winter was going off… this was the third year since he had been made king at Rome”; “they bore a siege of five months”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard date 37 BC (some argue 36 BC). Antiquities 14.16.4 adds 'the third month… on the fast day'; War does not.
note: Herod's men and Sosius's centurions stormed the walls and took the Temple area; Herod paid off the Romans to stop the looting and kept foreigners out of the sanctuary.

title: Antigonus, last Hasmonean king, executed by Antony
native: after the capture of Jerusalem
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 37 BC (or 36 BC).
note: Sosius took Antigonus in chains to Antony, who had him beheaded, ending Hasmonean rule.

title: Great earthquake in Judea kills 30,000
native: “in the seventh year of his reign, when the war about Actium was at the height, at the beginning of the spring”
conversion: Spring of 31 BC (the Actium campaign); Josephus gives the season, not the month.
note: The quake killed many cattle and about 30,000 people, but not Herod's army camped in the open. Archaeologists often link damage at Khirbet Qumran to it.

title: Herod meets Octavian at Rhodes and is confirmed as king
native: after Actium; “he sailed to Rhodes, where Caesar then abode”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Spring 30 BC.
note: Herod came without his diadem, admitted his loyalty to Antony, and was crowned again by Octavian.

title: Herod rebuilds Samaria as Sebaste
native: named “from Sebastus, or Augustus”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. 27 BC.
note: Herod settled 6,000 colonists in the city and built a temple to Augustus.

title: Herod begins rebuilding the Temple (15th year)
native: “in the fifteenth year of his reign, Herod rebuilt the temple”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 15th year from 37 BC ≈ 23/22 BC; Antiquities' 18th year ≈ 20/19 BC is the date more often cited.
note: Herod doubled the Temple enclosure, built new cloisters and rebuilt the fortress Antonia. War's 15th year differs from the 18th year in Antiquities 15.11.1.

title: Caesarea Maritima dedicated with games (192nd Olympiad)
native: “he first himself proposed the largest prizes upon the hundred ninety-second olympiad”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Olympiad 192 = 12–8 BC; the dedication is usually dated 10/9 BC.
note: Herod rebuilt Strato's Tower as Caesarea with a harbour bigger than the Piraeus, and founded five-yearly games for Caesar.

title: Herod has his sons Alexander and Aristobulus strangled at Sebaste
native: “he also sent his sons to Sebaste… and ordered them to be there strangled”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. 7 BC.
note: Mariamne's two sons were executed on Herod's order after a hearing at Berytus, and buried at Alexandrium.

title: Students cut down Herod's golden eagle from the Temple gate
native: when “a rumor was spread abroad that the king was dying”; done “at midday”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 4 BC on the standard chronology (1 BC on the alternative).
note: Followers of the teachers Judas and Matthias cut down the eagle. Herod had the teachers and the young men who did it burned alive. Antiquities ties this to the eclipse already in the app.

title: Death of Herod the Great, five days after executing Antipater
native: “having survived the slaughter of his son five days… reigned thirty-four years since he had caused Antigonus to be slain… thirty-seven years since he had been made king by the Romans”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Standard 4 BC (between the eclipse and Passover); some argue 1 BC.
note: Herod died at Jericho and was carried 200 furlongs to Herodium for burial. His reign lengths (34 years and 37 years) are the basis of the 4 BC date.

title: Archelaus's troops kill 3,000 at Passover
native: “at the feast of unleavened bread, which was now at hand, and is by the Jews called the Passover”
conversion: Passover (Nisan), the spring after Herod's death; 4 BC on the standard chronology.
note: Mourners for the men Herod burned rioted. Archelaus sent in the army, which killed about 3,000 around the Temple, and the feast was cancelled.

title: Pentecost revolt against Sabinus; Temple cloisters burned
native: “when that feast, which was observed after seven weeks, and which the Jews called Pentecost… was at hand”
conversion: Pentecost (Sivan), 4 BC.
note: Pilgrims besieged the procurator Sabinus. The Romans burned the Temple cloisters and robbed the treasury of up to 400 talents.

title: Varus crushes the revolt and crucifies 2,000
native: after Varus marched on Jerusalem
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 4 BC.
note: The Syrian legate Varus burned Sepphoris and Emmaus and crucified 2,000 rebels around Jerusalem.

title: Augustus divides Herod's kingdom among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip
native: after the hearing “in Apollo's temple” at Rome
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. 4 BC.
note: Archelaus received half the kingdom as ethnarch; Antipas got Galilee and Perea, and Philip Batanea and Trachonitis.

title: Archelaus banished to Vienne; Judea becomes a Roman province
native: “in the ninth year of his government he was banished to Vienna, a city of Gaul”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 6. War says the ninth year, Antiquities the tenth.
note: After complaints from Jews and Samaritans, Augustus deposed Archelaus. Judea came under the procurator Coponius.

title: Simon the Essene interprets Archelaus's dream of nine ears of corn
native: shortly “before he was sent for by Caesar”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 6.
note: Simon read the nine ears as nine years of rule and the oxen as a change of fortune. Five days later Archelaus was summoned to Caesar.

title: Judas the Galilean leads a revolt against the Roman tax (census of Quirinius)
native: “under his [Coponius's] administration”; “when Cyrenius was sent into Judea to make [a taxation]” (7.8.1)
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 6, the census of Quirinius.
note: Judas called it cowardice to pay tribute and accept mortal masters after God. He founded the 'fourth philosophy'; his descendants Menahem and Eleazar led the Sicarii.

title: Death of Augustus; Tiberius succeeds
native: Augustus “had reigned fifty-seven years, six months, and two days”
conversion: Julian date from Roman sources (Suetonius); Josephus gives only the length of the reign.
note: Josephus reports the succession; Philip and Antipas kept their tetrarchies.

title: Antipas founds Tiberias; Philip builds Caesarea Philippi and Julias
native: after Tiberius's accession
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Tiberias c. AD 18–20; Caesarea Philippi c. 3–2 BC onward.
note: Philip built Caesarea at the springs of the Jordan (Paneas) and Julias; Antipas built Tiberias in Galilee and another Julias in Perea.

title: Pilate brings Caesar's images into Jerusalem; the people bare their necks
native: “Pilate, who was sent as procurator into Judea by Tiberius”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Early in Pilate's term (AD 26–36), usually AD 26.
note: Crowds lay before Pilate's house at Caesarea for five days and nights. When surrounded by soldiers they offered their necks, and Pilate removed the standards.

title: Pilate spends the Temple treasure (Corban) on an aqueduct
native: “After this he raised another disturbance, by expending that sacred treasure which is called Corban upon aqueducts”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Sometime in AD 26–36; the year is unknown and AD 30 is a placeholder.
note: Soldiers disguised in the crowd beat the protesters at his tribunal, and many died.

title: Tiberius dies; Gaius frees Agrippa and makes him king
native: “until Tiberius died, after he had reigned twenty-two years, six months, and three days”
conversion: Julian date of Tiberius's death from Roman sources (Tacitus, Suetonius).
note: Agrippa, jailed six months for wishing Gaius emperor, was released and given Philip's tetrarchy with the title of king.

title: Herod Antipas banished to Spain; his tetrarchy given to Agrippa
native: Herod [Antipas] “was banished… into Spain”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 39. War says Spain; Antiquities says Lugdunum in Gaul.
note: Pushed by Herodias to seek a crown, Antipas was accused by Agrippa and exiled by Gaius.

title: Gaius orders his statue set up in the Temple; Petronius delays
native: the people stayed idle “for fifty days together” “about seed time”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 39/40; the protest was in the autumn sowing season, AD 40.
note: Jews massed before Petronius rather than allow the statue. He risked his life by writing to Gaius, and the order lapsed when Gaius was killed.

title: Gaius (Caligula) assassinated; Claudius made emperor
native: “when Caius had reigned three years and eight months, and had been slain by treachery”
conversion: Julian date from Roman sources; Josephus gives the length of the reign.
note: Agrippa I helped negotiate between Claudius and the Senate.

title: Claudius gives Agrippa I all of Herod's kingdom
native: “he bestowed on Agrippa his whole paternal kingdom immediately”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 41.
note: Claudius added Judea, Samaria and the kingdom of Lysanias, and gave Chalcis to Agrippa's brother Herod.

title: Agrippa I begins Jerusalem's third (north) wall
native: “he began to encompass Jerusalem with such a wall…”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 41–44.
note: Josephus says the wall would have made the city impregnable had it been finished; Agrippa's death stopped the work.

title: Death of Agrippa I at Caesarea
native: “He had then reigned three years, as he had governed his tetrarchies three other years”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 44.
note: Judea returned to procurators (Cuspius Fadus, then Tiberius Alexander). This is the death described in Acts 12:20–23.

title: Soldier's insult at Passover under Cumanus; crush kills 10,000
native: “when the multitude were come together to Jerusalem, to the feast of unleavened bread”
conversion: Passover (Nisan); Cumanus was procurator AD 48–52, so the year is about AD 48–49.
note: A soldier on the Temple cloister exposed himself to the crowd. The riot and panic that followed killed ten thousand (Antiquities: 20,000).

title: A Roman soldier tears and burns a Torah scroll
native: “a certain soldier, finding the sacred book of the law, tore it to pieces”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. AD 48–50.
note: After a robbery on the road, a soldier destroyed a Torah scroll in a village raid. Cumanus beheaded him to stop the uproar.

title: Galilean pilgrim killed at Geman on the way to Tabernacles
native: “as a great number of Jews were going up to Jerusalem to the feast [of tabernacles]”
conversion: Tabernacles (Tishri); about AD 51/52.
note: The killing led to Jewish–Samaritan fighting. Quadratus investigated, and Claudius banished Cumanus and had the tribune Celer executed in Jerusalem.

title: Claudius dies; Nero succeeds
native: “Claudius… when he had administered the government thirteen years, eight months, and twenty days, died”
conversion: Julian date from Roman sources.
note: Josephus notes the adoption of Nero through Agrippina. Felix was procurator, and Agrippa II was given Philip's former tetrarchy.

title: Sicarii murder the former high priest Jonathan
native: “The first man who was slain by them was Jonathan the high priest”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Under Felix (AD 52–60), c. AD 56.
note: The Sicarii hid daggers under their clothes and killed people in festival crowds; after Jonathan, many were killed every day.

title: The Egyptian false prophet's march to the Mount of Olives
native: under Felix
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. AD 55–57.
note: He gathered thousands (War: 30,000) to storm Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives; Felix routed them and he escaped. The tribune in Acts 21:38 mistakes Paul for him.

title: Jews and Syrians fight over citizenship at Caesarea
native: under Felix
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. AD 59–60.
note: The fight over whether Herod's Caesarea was a Jewish or Greek city reached Nero; his ruling for the Greeks became an immediate cause of the war (2.14.4).

title: Jesus son of Ananus begins crying “Woe to Jerusalem” at Tabernacles
native: “four years before the war began… came to that feast whereon it is our custom for every one to make tabernacles”
conversion: Tabernacles (15–21 Tishri) of AD 62, four years before the war; Albinus's term confirms the year.
note: A farmer cried against the city and Temple day and night for seven years and five months. Albinus had him flogged to the bone and released him as a madman.

title: Gessius Florus becomes procurator
native: “Gessius Florus who succeeded him [Albinus]”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 64.
note: Josephus calls him the worst procurator, who openly shared in robbers' spoils and 'forced the Jews into the war'.

title: Cestius Gallus visits Jerusalem at Passover; crowds denounce Florus
native: “upon the approach of the feast of unleavened bread”
conversion: Passover (Nisan) AD 66; some date it to AD 65.
note: Josephus says three million people appealed to Cestius against Florus, who laughed. Cestius used the Passover lambs to count the pilgrims (6.9.3).

title: A star like a sword over the city and a comet for a year
native: “there was a star resembling a sword, which stood over the city, and a comet, that continued a whole year”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Josephus does not date it; it is placed before the war (Halley's comet appeared early AD 66).
note: The first of the portents Josephus lists. Some identify the comet with Halley's comet of AD 66.

title: Great light shines round the altar at Passover, 8 Xanthicus
native: “on the eighth day of the month Xanthicus, [Nisan,] and at the ninth hour of the night”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. 'Before the Jews' rebellion' = Passover season AD 66 (some say 65). Ninth hour of the night ≈ 3 a.m. at the end of the night of 8 Nisan.
note: For half an hour the Temple shone as bright as day. At the same feast a heifer led to sacrifice gave birth to a lamb in the Temple.

title: The Temple's heavy brass eastern gate opens by itself
native: “at the same festival… was seen to be opened of its own accord about the sixth hour of the night”
conversion: Same Passover as the light at the altar (AD 66 or 65); Josephus gives the festival and the hour, not the day.
note: The gate normally needed twenty men to shut it. The learned took it to mean the Temple's protection was gone.

title: Chariots and armed troops seen in the clouds, 21 Artemisius
native: “a few days after that feast, on the one and twentieth day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,]… before sun-setting”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. Same spring as the Passover portents (AD 66 or 65).
note: Josephus says it would seem a fable if eyewitnesses had not reported it: armies running among the clouds and surrounding cities.

title: Priests hear a voice at Pentecost: “Let us remove hence”
native: “at that feast which we call Pentecost, as the priests were going by night into the inner [court]”
conversion: Pentecost (Sivan) of the same year as the other portents (AD 66 or 65).
note: The priests felt a quaking, heard a great noise, and then the sound of a multitude saying 'Let us remove hence'.

title: War begins at Caesarea: birds sacrificed at the synagogue on the Sabbath
native: “the war began, in the twelfth year of the reign of Nero, and the seventeenth of the reign of Agrippa, in the month of Artemisius [Jyar]”; “the next day, which was the seventh day of the week”
conversion: Artemisius (Iyar) in Nero's 12th year (Oct 65–Oct 66) = spring AD 66; the Sabbath falls in early Iyar.
note: After Nero ruled for the Greeks, a Greek sacrificed birds on an upturned pot at the synagogue entrance on the Sabbath. The fighting that followed was Josephus's formal start of the war.

title: Florus plunders the Upper Market; 3,600 killed and Jewish knights crucified
native: “This happened upon the sixteenth day of the month Artemisius [Jyar]”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date.
note: After taking 17 talents from the Temple treasury and being mocked, Florus let his troops loose on the Upper Market. He scourged and crucified Jews of equestrian rank, which Josephus calls unprecedented.

title: Queen Bernice pleads barefoot before Florus
native: “about this very time”; she she “stood barefoot before Florus's tribunal, and besought him [to spare the Jews]”
conversion: Same days as the massacre of 16 Artemisius, AD 66.
note: Bernice was in Jerusalem for a Nazirite vow. Florus ignored her, and soldiers killed people in front of her.

title: Agrippa II's speech urging Jerusalem not to fight Rome
native: after Neopolitanus's visit
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Early summer AD 66 (between Iyar and Lous).
note: Agrippa listed the nations Rome had conquered and warned that war would destroy the city and Temple. The people later drove him out.

title: Rebels seize Masada and kill its Roman garrison
native: “at this time it was that some… made an assault upon a certain fortress called Masada”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Summer AD 66, before Lous.
note: The fortress was taken by treachery. Menahem later armed his followers from Herod's armoury there.

title: Sacrifice for Caesar stopped: “the true beginning of our war”
native: “this was the true beginning of our war with the Romans; for they rejected the sacrifice of Caesar”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Summer AD 66 (some scholars put it in Panemus/Tammuz), before the Xylophory of Lous.
note: The Temple captain Eleazar persuaded the priests to accept no gift or sacrifice from a foreigner, ending the daily offering for the emperor.

title: Wood-carrying feast: rebels burn the high priest's house and debt archives
native: “the next day was the festival of Xylophory; upon which the custom was for every one to bring wood for the altar”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. Josephus puts the Xylophory the day before 15 Lous, giving 14 Av (the Mishnah's main wood-offering day is 15 Av).
note: With the Sicarii, the rebels drove the king's troops from the upper city and burned the houses of Ananias, Agrippa and Bernice and the archives, destroying the records of debts.

title: Rebels take the Antonia after a two-day siege and burn it
native: “on the next day, which was the fifteenth of the month Lous, [Ab,] they made an assault upon Antonia… besieged the garrison… two days”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. The assault began 15 Av; the fall came two days later (≈17 Av).
note: The garrison was killed and the citadel burned. The rebels then besieged Herod's palace.

title: Menahem's men burn the Roman camp; the garrison flees to Herod's towers

AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).
note: The defenders filled the roof of the western cloister with wood, bitumen and pitch and pretended to retreat. Many Romans who climbed it died in the fire.

title: Famine: Mary of Bethezob eats her own child
native: “There was a certain woman that dwelt beyond Jordan, her name was Mary”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Narrated between 27 Panemus and 8 Lous, AD 70.
note: Josephus tells it as the worst horror of the famine, recalling the curses of Deuteronomy 28:56–57. It hardened Titus's resolve.

title: Banks completed against the Temple; Titus orders the gates set on fire
native: “two of the legions had completed their banks on the eighth day of the month Lous [Ab]”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).
note: The rams failed against the Temple walls, so the gates were burned. The next day Titus's council argued over whether to spare the sanctuary.

title: Roman standards set up in the Temple court; Titus hailed imperator
native: “brought their ensigns to the temple and set them over against its eastern gate; and there did they offer sacrifices to them”
conversion: Immediately after the Temple burned (10 Lous), Av AD 70.
note: The legions sacrificed to their standards in the Temple court. Loot was so plentiful that gold sold in Syria at half its value.

title: Titus parleys with Simon and John at the Xystus bridge
native: “he placed himself on the western side of the outer [court of the] temple… above the Xystus”
conversion: Av AD 70, shortly after the Temple fell.
note: The tyrants asked to leave with their families for the desert. Titus refused and ordered the city burned and plundered.

title: Lower city burned as far as Siloam
native: “the Romans drove the robbers out of the lower city, and set all on fire as far as Siloam”
conversion: Av AD 70.
note: The archives, the council house and the Ophel quarter were burned; the rebels held only the upper city.

title: Titus begins banks against the upper city
native: “this on the twentieth day of the month Lous [Ab]”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).
note: Timber had to be brought from 100 furlongs away. The Idumaeans tried to negotiate a surrender.

title: Priests hand over Temple treasures to Titus
native: “one of the priests, the son of Thebuthus, whose name was Jesus”
conversion: Between 20 Lous and 7 Gorpiaeus AD 70.
note: Jesus son of Thebuthi gave up two candlesticks, tables, bowls and the priestly vestments; the treasurer Phineas surrendered the priests' garments and spices.

title: Banks finished and the upper city wall breached
native: “now were the banks finished on the seventh day of the month Gorpieus, [Elul,] in eighteen days' time”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).
note: The rebels lost heart, left the towers of Hippicus, Phasael and Mariamne, and fled into the valley under Siloam and the tunnels.

title: Jerusalem taken on 8 Gorpiaeus
native: “thus was Jerusalem taken, in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, on the eighth day of the month Gorpeius [Elul]”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).
note: The whole city was taken and burned. Josephus says it had been taken five times before and desolated twice, 2,177 years after its founding by Melchizedek and 1,179 years after David.

title: Josephus's totals: 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead
native: “the number of those that were carried captive during this whole war was… ninety-seven thousand… those that perished during the whole siege eleven hundred thousand”
conversion: Summary given after the fall (Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70).
note: He explains the numbers by the Passover crowds. A census by paschal lambs under Cestius had counted 256,500 sacrifices, about 2.7 million people.

title: Jesus son of Ananus killed by a siege stone, still crying “Woe”
native: after “seven years and five months”: “Woe, woe to myself also!”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. During the siege, AD 70 (7 years 5 months from Tabernacles AD 62 points to about spring 70).
note: On the wall he cried 'Woe to me also' and was killed by a stone from a Roman engine.

title: John of Gischala gives himself up from the tunnels
native: “As for John, he wanted food, together with his brethren, in these caverns, and begged that the Romans would now give him their right hand”; “John condemned to perpetual imprisonment”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Shortly after 8 Gorpiaeus, AD 70.
note: John, starved out, surrendered and was sentenced to life imprisonment; 2,000 dead were found in the tunnels.

title: Titus orders the city and Temple razed; three towers and the west wall left
native: “Caesar gave orders that they should now demolish the entire city and temple, but… leave… Phasaelus, and Hippicus, and Mariamne”
conversion: Right after the capture, Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70.
note: The rest was levelled so that visitors would not believe it had been inhabited. The 10th Legion stayed as the garrison.

title: Simon bar Giora rises from the ground in white and purple on the Temple site
native: Simon “put on a white frock… and appeared out of the ground in the place where the temple had formerly been”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Autumn AD 70, while Titus was at Caesarea.
note: After failing to tunnel out, Simon tried to frighten the guards. He was chained and kept for the triumph.

title: Titus marks Domitian's birthday at Caesarea; 2,500 captives killed
native: “he solemnized the birthday of his brother Domitian after a splendid manner”
conversion: Josephus gives no date. Domitian's birthday was 24 October (Suetonius), so 24 Oct 70.
note: Captives were killed fighting beasts, burned and made to fight each other.

title: Titus marks Vespasian's birthday at Berytus with more captive deaths
native: “exhibited a still more pompous solemnity about his father's birthday”
conversion: Josephus gives no date. Vespasian's birthday was 17 November (Suetonius), so 17 Nov 70.
note: There were more shows and many more captives died.

title: Antioch: the apostate Antiochus accuses the Jews and the Sabbath is suppressed
native: Antiochus was “not permitting them to rest on the seventh day”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Accusation c. AD 67; fire and petitions AD 70/71.
note: A renegade Jew accused his people of plotting to burn the city, which led to killings and a ban on Sabbath rest. After a real fire (AD 70/71) Titus refused to expel the Jews.

title: Triumph of Vespasian and Titus in Rome; Simon bar Giora executed
native: the procession ending “at the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 71 (June 71 from other sources; Josephus gives no month).
note: The Temple spoils were carried, including the golden table, the lampstand and a copy of the Law. Simon was dragged to the Forum and executed.

title: Temple tax diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus; veterans settled at Emmaus
native: “enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 71.
note: Vespasian kept Judea as his own property, settled 800 veterans at Emmaus (Motza), and imposed the Jewish tax (fiscus Judaicus).

title: Lucilius Bassus takes Herodium
native: Bassus “took that citadel which was in Herodium”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 71.
note: This began the mopping-up of the last rebel strongholds.

title: Machaerus surrenders to save the young Eleazar from crucifixion
native: Bassus “resolved to besiege it, by filling up the valley that lay on the east side”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 71/72. Machaerus is where Antiquities places John the Baptist's death; War does not mention him.
note: After the captured Eleazar was scourged and a cross set up in sight of the walls, the garrison gave up the fortress in exchange for his life. The Romans then killed the 'strangers' in the lower town.

title: Bassus destroys 3,000 fugitives in the forest of Jardes
native: “he marched hastily to the forest of Jarden, as it is called”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 72.
note: Fugitives from Jerusalem and Machaerus were surrounded and killed, including Judas son of Ari.

title: Antiochus IV of Commagene deposed (fourth year of Vespasian)
native: “in the fourth year of the reign of Vespasian”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Vespasian's 4th year = July 72–July 73; usually AD 72.
note: Caesennius Paetus accused him of plotting with Parthia; his kingdom was annexed.

title: The Alans invade Media and Armenia
native: “This nation about this time laid a design of falling upon Media”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. c. AD 72.
note: The Alans came through the Caspian Gates, plundered Media and nearly lassoed King Tiridates of Armenia.

title: Flavius Silva besieges Masada
native: “Flavius Silva succeeded him as procurator… made an expedition against it”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Winter AD 72/73 (or 73/74).
note: Silva walled Masada round and built a ramp on the White Promontory against Eleazar son of Jair's Sicarii.

title: Masada falls: 960 die by their own hands, 15 Xanthicus
native: “This calamitous slaughter was made on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus [Nisan]”
conversion: Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. The year is disputed: AD 73 is traditional, AD 74 is favoured by many since inscriptions show Silva governing into 73/74. AD 74 gives ≈ 1 Apr 74 on this reckoning; other calendar readings (e.g. Tyrian) put it some weeks later.
note: After Eleazar's speeches the defenders killed their families and then each other, and burned everything but the food. Two women and five children hid and survived.

title: Sicarii fugitives in Alexandria handed over; they refuse to call Caesar lord
native: “not one of these children was so far overcome by these torments, as to name Caesar for their lord”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 73 (or 74, depending on Masada's date).
note: The Jewish elders handed over 600 Sicarii. Under torture none would call Caesar lord, which Josephus admired.

title: Vespasian has the temple of Onias in Egypt closed
native: “the duration of the time from the building of this temple till it was shut up again was three hundred and forty-three years”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 73 or 74. Josephus's 343 years conflicts with a founding c. 160 BC (should be ≈ 230).
note: Lupus and then Paulinus took the offerings, shut the gates and stopped all worship there.

title: Jonathan the weaver leads a desert movement in Cyrene
native: “one Jonathan, a vile person, and by trade a weaver”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. AD 73–74.
note: Jonathan promised signs in the desert, and the governor Catullus crushed them. Catullus then killed 3,000 wealthy Jews, and Jonathan falsely accused Josephus in Rome.

title: Vespasian's Temple of Peace receives the Temple's gold vessels
native: “he also laid up therein those golden vessels and instruments that were taken out of the Jewish temple”
conversion: Year only; Josephus gives no month or day here. Dedicated AD 75 (Cassius Dio); Josephus gives no year.
note: The Law and the purple veils of the sanctuary were kept in the palace.
